components.source_comparison: p. 116: weak convergence of distribution functions at continuity points of the limit, convergence in distribution of random variables via their distribution functions, and the remark that continuity points suffice to identify the limit (the last is supplied in C003). Handbook supplies both definitions, the no-common-space reading, equality in distribution and the proper-CDF conditions.

p. 118: Y_n(x)=sup{y:F_n(y)<x} on ((0,1), Borel, Lebesgue), the F^{-1} notation, a_x=sup{y:F(y)<x}, b_x=inf{y:F(y)>x}. Handbook defines Q_F, a_F, b_F with the source's strict convention, identifies F^{-1}(u)=Q_F(u), fixes the uniform space and excludes u=0,1.

p. 116 remark (right continuity plus countably many discontinuities, Exercise 1.2.3, identify the limit) and p. 118 appeal to Theorem 1.2.2 (Y_n has distribution F_n). Annex writes the countable-jump proof, density of continuity points, uniqueness of the proper weak limit, finiteness and order of a_F, b_F, the inf form of Q_F, the ray identity, measurability and the pushforward CDF; law uniqueness cites the existing thm:p15-cdf-laws (measurable-probability.tex 427).

pp. 118-119 Theorem 3.2.8: statement, exceptional set Omega-Omega_0 countable via disjoint intervals each holding a rational, parts (a) liminf and (b) limsup via continuity points. All present with written steps; boundary that joint laws are not preserved is stated (lines 83-84).

p. 119: Theorem 3.2.9 with coupling proof and ramp converse (both written, AP 101-141); the introducing claim that the result 'gives an equivalent definition of weak convergence that makes sense in any topological space' is supplied only in the owned file (definition on a topological space, finiteness of the integrals, coincidence on the line, continuous images, uniqueness under a metric, two-point non-uniqueness, warning on what transfers). Worked boundary: unbounded test function (BP 450-453).
components.note: The topological-space remark is covered only by the packet's new owned files; route pending (rule S9).

components.source_comparison: p. 120 Theorem 3.2.10, its Remark (D_g always Borel, Exercise 1.3.6), the f-composition proof and the bounded second conclusion. Annex proves D_g is F-sigma for arbitrary finite real g and also by the envelope route, then the composition argument and the bounded case. Boundary g=1_{0} at BP 443-445 / AP 861-864.
p. 121: K = closure, G = interior, boundary = closure minus interior, continuity set via P(X_inf in boundary A)=0. Present.

pp. 120-121 Theorem 3.2.11 (i)-(iv), the four source implications (i)=>(ii), (ii)<=>(iii), (ii)+(iii)=>(iv), (iv)=>(i) all written, with the cycle closed. The Remark (point masses x_n in G converging to a boundary point; K=G^c for (iii)) appears on the route only as the instance delta_{1/n}, G=(0,inf), K=(-inf,0]; its general form is proved only in the owned file (boundary-approach theorem (i)-(v)).
components.note: The general form of the source Remark after Theorem 3.2.11 is covered only by the packet's new owned files; route pending (rule S9).

components.source_comparison: p. 121 Remark: the limit may not be a distribution function; the convergence is sometimes called vague and denoted =>_v. Handbook defines the Helly CDF limit, the =>_v reading, beta and gamma, and the properness condition.

pp. 121-122 Theorem 3.2.12: diagonal argument over enumerated rationals (with the scalar selection premise written), F(x)=inf{G(q):q>x} and its right continuity, continuity-point argument with r1<r2<x<s. The Remark's mixture a1(x>=n)+b1(x>=-n)+cG(x), its endpoint limits b and b+c=1-a, and mass a escaping to +inf and b to -inf: BP 193-194 and 458-467 with proof AP 886-897.
p. 122: tight iff for all eps there is M with limsup_n 1-F_n(M)+F_n(-M) <= eps. Present in the source form, with the included left endpoint stated and the uniform variant (proved in C012).

p. 122 Theorem 3.2.13, both directions as in the source (continuity points r<-M, s>M; non-tight subsequence n(k) with H_{n(k)}(k)>=eps and a further Helly subsequence). Annex also proves the uniform-tail equivalence, the further-subsequence formulation and tightness of weakly convergent sequences. Worked boundary: mixture tight exactly when a=b=0 (BP 466-467, AP 893-897).

p. 123 Theorem 3.2.14 (phi>=0, phi(x)->inf as |x|->inf, C=sup_n int phi dF_n finite) and its bound 1-F_n(M)+F_n(-M) <= C/inf_{|x|>=M} phi. Handbook's coercivity is equivalent to phi->inf, adds the needed measurability, allows infinite values, gives the C/L bound and handles C=0.

p. 124 Exercises 3.2.6 (Levy rho with the source's inf form) and 3.2.7 (Ky Fan alpha=inf{eps>=0: P(|X-Y|>eps)<=eps}). Both defined as in the source, with a.s. identification and the metric/convergence vocabulary.

p. 124: Ex 3.2.6 (rho a metric; rho(F_n,F)->0 iff F_n=>F, both directions written), Ex 3.2.7 (rho(F,G)<=alpha(X,Y), written with the attained infimum), Ex 3.2.12 (convergence in probability implies in distribution; X_n=>c implies convergence in probability via the closed-set portmanteau bound); p. 123 sentence that these exercises give metrics for convergence in distribution. Worked boundary: fair sign X_n=-X (BP 446-449, AP 866-869).

p. 123 Theorem 3.2.15 and its justification ('convergence in distribution comes from a metric'): the metric route is written from the proved Levy premises, plus a direct CDF route and the tightness/unique-limit method.

p. 117: total variation norm ||mu_n-mu_inf|| = sup_B |mu_n(B)-mu_inf(B)|. Defined in the source's supremum-over-events convention, with the half-L1 relation stated and phi, Phi fixed with normalization from thm:p15-normal-normalization.

p. 117 Scheffe: Borel-set bound, the identity int|f_n-f_inf| = 2 int (f_inf-f_n)^+ from f_n>=0 with integral one, dominated convergence, TV norm -> 0, 'stronger than weak convergence (take B=(-inf,x])', and point mass at 1/n with TV distance 1. Handbook proves the general a.e. version, records the source's pointwise Lebesgue-density case as a special case, proves the exact half-L1 TV identity and the weak-convergence consequence; delta_{1/n} at BP 439-440 and the normalization boundary at BP 454-457.

Premises the Section 3.2 examples take from Section 3.1: Lemma 3.1.1 (Example 3.2.4, scalar form), Exercise 3.1.1 (Example 3.2.5, array form) and the P(S_2n=0) asymptotic of Theorem 3.1.2 (Example 3.2.6). Array and scalar product limits and C_n sqrt(pi n) -> 1 are proved with written steps (log remainder; cosine-power recursion, dominated convergence, Gaussian integral).

p. 116 Example 3.2.1 (the source invokes Theorem 3.1.3). The needed limit is proved in full: local binomial masses uniformly on bounded scaled ranges, Riemann sums with endpoint control, Chebyshev tail, and odd N; the Theorem 3.1.3 route itself is pointed to at BP 475-476 (thm:p15-stirling-de-moivre-laplace exists, de-moivre-laplace-and-stirling.tex 163).

pp. 116-117 Examples 3.2.2 (Glivenko-Cantelli, convergence for all y even with discontinuities; uses existing thm:p15-glivenko-cantelli), 3.2.3 (F(x-1/n) -> F(x-), why continuity points), 3.2.4 (P(X_p>=n)=(1-p)^{n-1}, pX_p => exponential via Lemma 3.1.1), 3.2.5 (product formula, limit exp(-x^2/2) via Exercise 3.1.1, N=365 arithmetic). The on-route chapter gives both numerical values but not the source's reading (probability that no two of n people share a birthday, equal-likelihood assumption) or its '2% smaller than the true probability 0.524' comparison; those are supplied, with the comparison proved (1.71%-1.74%), only in the owned file.
